comments.text:
Well, it seems that the B580 is getting plenty of love from other reviewers; which I am genuinely happy about; as we absolutely need this ARC GPU to succeed to bring affordable gaming to more people.

Now, the big question is - "Why are you the only channel that doesn't like this?!" Well, as we see in the video, I had serious issues with Ghosts and Dragon Age, then in the benchmarking process, CS2 and PC2. This meant that of the games tested across three PCs (and yes a clean install on one of them), Four games had big problems. Plus warnings in Halo and Returnal that you have an incompatible GPU. Good to great performance in the rest.

Intel also emailed us with a new driver after the initial film, as follows: 
"We will post a new driver Dec 9, Monday morning Pacific Time. This driver will ONLY contain the below app-specific fixes:
Dragon Age: The Veilgard corruption and crash fixes
Ghost of Tsushima improved frametimes
Star Wars Outlaws crash fix
Black Myth: Wukong performance and crash fixes with ray tracing enabled
God of War Ragnarok texture fix
F1 24 improved frametimes
Genshin Impact crash fix"

After this, I then retested the games, and rebenchmarked the card, for the numbers you see here - so a weeks worth of testing.

I appreciate that my results are different to others out there, but it is my job to report on my experience, warts and all. How could I post a video saying that this is a perfect card, and you should all buy one, when I had these issues, of which CS and PC2 are currently unresolved? 

Anything but the my honest experience would be disingenuous to you, and this video reflects my week with the ARC card. You are welcome to disagree with my verdict, but in my opinion, it is a wise choice to wait to see how this card fares after a couple of months of maturity. 

I love you all - and will always give you the honest truth - it would be a lot easier to say this is great, and to run out and buy it, but that wouldn't be reflective of my experience. Thanks for listening to my ted talk.

As someone who has been using an Arc A770 for 6-7 months now after upgrading from a Vega 64 and the B580 since release day, I absolutely agree Arc isn't for the average consumer yet. I'm hopeful for the future of Arc too, but I think it'll take at least until Druid releases for it to become viable for the average PC gamer.

comments.text:
Expecting a new card to have flawless drivers at launch is dumb. Neither AMD nor Nvidia have had flawless drivers at launch in recent memory either, so dunking on Intel for this isn't fair. 

Intel released an updated driver prior to launch for reviewers only, which means the issues you faced with GoT and DA: Failguard weren't representative of a new user's experience. It's a failure on the reviewer's part to not address this before commentating on it and making an inaccurate conclusion for end users. Intel is at fault too for releasing an updated driver so close to release date but then again, this is a reviewer issue only and it was expected of a GPU brand that is only on it's second generation and trying to catch up to several decades worth of progress in just a few years, so some amount of consideration should've been held. 

The issue with relatively lower framerate in CSGO2 isn't as big of a deal, as you stated, but you also blew it's significance out of proportion when the card is clearly performing way better in other games where the difference in framerate actually matters. 100 less frames when you're getting 250-350 isn't the end of the world, therefore the statement "you wanna get what you pay for" doesn't feel right. That, or I am definitely not getting what I'm paying for on a 4060 with it's paltry 8GB memory, which makes FG and high settings unusable in plenty of games - no mention of that, gee I wonder why.

There were several points in the video where the B580 was clearly the far superior choice, but the overall negative tone of the video continued throughout and failed to acknowledge the positives. As a reviewer you also failed to address the highly relevant VRAM issue in other cards at the $300 and below price point, which this card clearly tackles. 

Your final conclusion is less biased but as a viewer it's a little too late. My impression on the card is already in the negative, thanks to inaccurate results earlier in the video, and your multiple attempts to sell me the 4060 has made sure that I do not consider the B580 as my first choice. 

At the end of the day as a reviewer you reserve your rights to your own opinion, but that opinion should've been better informed. I do not believe one negative review out of dozens of positive reviews makes the negative review inaccurate, because it is entirely possible to have a different experience with a different set of parameters from everyone else. But as I said, it should've been better informed. Do better next time.

comments.text:
I still play on 1080p60 native. I really only see myself ever going as high as 1440, but 1080 is perfectly fine. But it's weird how some powerful cards today still kinda struggle reaching 1080p60 without DLSS. 4090 can barely play Portal RTX and Stalker 2 RT at 1080p60 with DLSS off, and I feel like that kinda says something about the state of optimization. To be honest I almost feel like developers rely a little too much on DLSS a a whole, and large amounts of RAM and VRAM, to deal with all the unneeded bloat.

I'm on a 1660 Ti myself. Make no mistake, it's still a beast of a card and can play plenty of games and VR perfectly fine (I can literally max out Half-Life Alyx on it). But because a lot of games today rely so much on DLSS, fake AI optimization, and excess VRAM, a game that could very easily run on my GPU instead chugs like crazy, and it's disheartening.

I mean, hell... a lot of games I play now also use TAA and it looks blurry and causes smearing/ghosting. We have all this high fidelity stuff but it just looks blurry via all the post processing, which they then mask with a sharpening filter that looks crappier still.

Fidelity ≠ clarity.

All I'm saying is that we're focusing so much on GPU power and enhancements nowadays that we focus less on actual game optimization. DLSS should not be a method devs can use to be lazy. If people want to use it for ultra high resolutions at ultra high frame rates, go for it, but if you turn that stuff off and can't even get average performance at an average resolution, then optimizations are going to be needed on your game, especially if we want affordable midrange as well as older cards like mine (which are still powerful) to still thrive in PC gaming.

I'm glad we're finally getting some love in the midrange department, but it's going to take more than just hardware to improve the PC space. It feels like we reached a graphical peak (besides RT) in like 2016, anything more now is basically bloat, and BECAUSE there's so much bloat, we literally have to resort to downscaling and then faking it with AI just to get decent frames. And there's plenty of games from across the 2010s, or even older, where you can crank them to 4K and they look incredible, with sharpness and clarity, because they're not blurred with all the post processing and temporal ghosting.
